column8: - Ambiguous ownership is a growing liability for AI deployments; a formal shared-responsibility model is no longer optional · - AI-enabled systems exhibit probabilistic behaviors and novel risks (training data, user-generated content, model provider actions) unlike deterministic traditional software · - Traditional three-layer cloud shared-responsibility models do not address AI-specific concerns: regulatory accountability, training data governance, agentic boundaries, shadow AI · - The dependencies encoded in the five architecture layers remain invariant regardless of how an organization structures its teams · - Without layered accountability, the default outcome is a finger-pointing cycle where every party blames another · - Emerging agentic AI systems capable of semi-autonomous operation create accountability challenges beyond what prior frameworks addressed
column9: - There must be exactly one accountable party per activity or component; overlapping accountability is not permitted · - Security and governance requirements must always cascade from the Business layer down through every supporting layer · - All autonomous agents must retain immediate human intervention capability, regardless of autonomy level · - Organizations deploying agents at autonomy level L3 or above must document their autonomy classification and review it quarterly · - At full autonomy (L5), organizations must require contractual accountability clauses from agentic providers covering cross-domain decision outcomes · - Model providers must always publish and maintain model version and vulnerability disclosures
column10: - Exactly one accountable party per activity, the framework's core rule · - Five-layer enterprise architecture: AI Business & Usage, AI Information, AI Application, AI Platform, AI Model Provider · - Shared responsibility calibrated by operating model (AI-SaaS, AI-PaaS, Agent-PaaS, IaaS), with customer responsibility rising toward infrastructure-layer deployments · - Responsibility shifts by autonomy level, moving from end user toward application developer and agentic provider as agent autonomy increases (adapted SAE J3016 L0-L5 scale) · - Complementary, not competing, with NIST AI RMF (what to do) and ISO 42001 (how to manage it); CoSAI SRF defines who is accountable · - Evidence-based accountability: an implementation playbook with evidence requirements per layer, not just stated principles · - Tiered human-intervention authority, a graduated response scale up to CISO/executive-authorized emergency shutdown
